summary.title: Software Design is Knowledge Building
summary.one_liner: Software design is best understood as building a shared mental model (a theory) of a system and its domain, and losing that understanding, not the code, is what makes systems decay.
keywords: why legacy code is hard to change
takeaways: Code is not the main product of software development; the programmers' theory of the system and its mapping to the domain is.
When the people who hold that theory leave, the system can keep running but becomes hard or impossible to change intelligently (Naur's 'dead program').
Changes made without understanding the original design concept erode structure and make the system harder to maintain (Parnas's software aging).
Revival of a system is possible by rebuilding the theory, though it is slow; Naur thought revival from code and docs alone was impossible, which the author partly disputes.
Design decisions such as names, structure, and comments should be judged by how they help future developers build a mental model of the system and business.
summary.summary: The essay tells a fictionalized true story of an in-house replacement system (SVC) built by one engineer who then left, after which successive teams could not safely change it. It uses this case to argue, drawing on David Parnas's Software Aging paper and Peter Naur's Programming as Theory Building, that the primary product of software design is a shared mental model that explains how the code maps to the real world and why each part exists. The author compares this with Zach Tellman's view that software development is explanation and with the conventional view of minimizing complexity, finding them compatible. It closes by suggesting organizational knowledge building as the goal of design, and noting that code and paratexts like comments, READMEs and commit messages should serve future maintainers' understanding.
